title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0d...) to evaluate whether inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation produced per task and reused across arms; guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair). We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All archived scoring artifacts indicate safe outcomes in every paired episode: baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because the shared_initial_candidate semantics produced identical initial candidates that passed deterministic validation in every task, no validator‑triggered repairs occurred and the paired contrast is uninformative for the causal effect of the verifier in this run. We present the preregistered design, exact quantitative outcomes, an artifact‑grounded failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations to render future GVR paired tests informative.

sections.introduction:
Translating high‑level operator intent into safe device configurations is a core NetOps objective. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows can synthesize multi‑step configuration sequences, but textual fidelity alone does not guarantee ordering, dependency, or invariant preservation required for safe application in production networks. Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configurations are executed against device images or simulators and deterministically scored—exposes semantic failure modes (ordering errors, transient violations, protected‑resource touches) not visible in text‑only tests [1].

A widely proposed architectural remedy is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM produces a candidate configuration; a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants; and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations are detected [2,3]. Prior work shows GVR patterns can correct many syntactic and some semantic faults, but open questions remain about empirical verifier benefit under distribution shift and adversarial prompts, and about experimental designs that can produce informative paired contrasts between guarded and unguarded pipelines [2,4].

This paper reports a preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) that measured a single primary estimand: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline), where unsafe_apply indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. We executed under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms), archived full execution and analysis artifacts, and here present artifact‑grounded outcomes, interpretation, and recommendations for future GVR evaluations.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks have recently been developed to evaluate agentic NetOps behavior in closed‑loop settings rather than via text‑only proxies; NetConfArena is a recent example that motivates this study's emulation grounding [1]. Research on automated configuration repair and program repair documents the utility of generate–validate patterns and shows that validators frequently enable high repair coverage for many benchmarked faults, though semantic coverage depends on verifier design [2,4]. Survey and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising patterns for operational NetOps automation and safety [3,5]. Engineering work on configuration analysis tools such as Batfish demonstrates scalable verifier design principles and incremental verification practices relevant to runtime GVR integration [6].

Our study differs from prior work in three ways that affect interpretability: (a) it used a preregistered paired estimand; (b) it executed with shared_initial_candidate semantics so each task produced exactly one LLM candidate reused across arms; and (c) it archived per‑call traces, deterministic validator traces, and analysis artifacts to permit exact reconciliations between the preregistered estimand and produced outputs.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0d...). The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied; safe_apply = 0 otherwise. The analysis used a paired contingency approach with bootstrap 95% percentile confidence intervals and an exact McNemar two‑sided test for discordant pairs. Bootstrap parameters (resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729) were recorded in the analysis logs.

Design, tasks, and sampling: The design is paired under shared_initial_candidate generation semantics: the adapter produced exactly one initial LLM generation per task and both conditions used that same candidate; the guarded arm could invoke up to one validator‑triggered repair. We executed N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks blocked into topology/vendor clusters: in‑distribution = 144, distribution‑shift = 48, adversarial‑prompt = 48. Tasks were generated deterministically by the registered task generator and include explicit intent payloads, initial device states, required command sequences, and preserved‑field constraints; representative task manifests and task difficulty labels are archived to permit independent inspection.

Model, verifier, and adapter contract: Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini (as recorded in the run configuration) and the deterministic verifier deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Under the shared_initial_candidate contract, paired differences can only arise if the single shared candidate fails deterministic validation or if the guarded arm applies a repair that changes the final configuration relative to the baseline.

Scoring, exclusions, and missingness: Final outcomes are binary (safe vs unsafe) determined by execution against the emulation and the verifier's semantic checks. The preregistration defined exclusion rules: items flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (verifier PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) would be excluded from primary analysis and included in sensitivity analyses; infra failures after allowed retries would be excluded per policy. A deterministic reconciliation step audited provider call accounting, pair completeness, and missingness and recorded that there were no infra failures or unscorable episodes in this run.

Traceability checklist (high level): preregistration record → archived preregistration manifest; execution accounting and provider audit → archived execution manifest and reconciliation artifact; per‑task validator traces and shared initial responses → archived validator traces and response traces; primary analysis outputs (paired contingency, condition summary, bootstrap parameters) → archived analysis artifacts and analysis log. These artifact labels are preserved in the study bundle to enable independent verification without reproducing low‑level provenance in the prose.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed per the preregistered plan. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete paired tasks = 240. Provider call accounting recorded exactly one shared initial generation per task and model_calls_used = 240 consistent with the adapter contract. No infra failures, unscorable episodes, or preregistered exclusions occurred.

Primary binary outcomes and contingency: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Observed counts: baseline_success_count = 240, guarded_success_count = 240; baseline failures = 0; guarded failures = 0. Paired contingency (discordant pair counts) is n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These numeric artifacts are archived in the analysis outputs and analysis logs.

Validator activity and repair utilization: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied in this execution (repair attempts = 0). Representative validator traces archived with the run show validation_before/validation_after snapshots, final_state fields, required_command_count, and difficulty labels (e.g., "very_hard"/"extreme"); in each archived validator trace the shared initial candidate passed the verifier's checks and the final guarded configuration matched that shared candidate. Consequently, baseline and guarded outcomes are identical across all subgroups (in‑distribution, shift, adversarial).

Planned sensitivity channels that were unused: The preregistration specified sensitivity analyses for 'possible false‑safe' flags and infra failures (treating such items as unsafe in worst‑case analyses). No items were flagged and no infra failures occurred; contamination summaries are empty. Subgroup paired contrasts are degenerate (all zeros) and archived subgroup slices are available for inspection.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast: Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the adapter produced exactly one LLM candidate per task and both arms used that same candidate. Because deterministic_netops_validator_v5 passed every shared candidate and no repairs were invoked, the guarded arm could not create discordant pairs. The run's deterministic reconciliation confirms adherence to the shared_initial_candidate contract and provider call accounting; these archived facts mechanistically explain the degenerate contingency (n11 = 240, n10 = n01 = 0).

Design tradeoffs and implications: Shared_initial_candidate semantics reduce model‑call budget and produce a direct pairing of generator output, but they also prevent generator variability between arms. For a paired causal estimate of verifier benefit, the design must guarantee opportunities for the verifier to act (i.e., generator failures or independent arm generations). To make a future paired test informative, one or more of the following should be adopted: (A) allow independent initial generations per arm so generator variability can produce discordant initial candidates; (B) increase adversary strength or diversify adversarial seeds to produce generator failures that exercise the verifier and repair path; or (C) permit larger repair budgets and multi‑iteration repairs so the repair mechanism can be exercised when validation fails. These recommendations arise directly from the archived provider call accounting and validator traces that show identical shared initial responses and zero repair usage.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded): Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate contract is an explicit preregistered choice that restricts causal contrast interpretation; the execution manifest and reconciliation artifact document contract adherence. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks and may not cover all semantic fault classes; archived validator traces record observed_touched_field_count and violation_codes which permit diagnostic follow‑up. External validity: tasks were drawn from a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus and deterministically generated; extrapolation to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator procedures requires caution. Conclusion validity: the observed baseline unsafe rate = 0 in this run prevents detection of verifier benefit under the chosen design; future power planning must account for generator variability and adversary strength to ensure informative discordant pairs.

Operational guidance: For practitioners aiming to evaluate or deploy GVR pipelines, we recommend (1) selecting experimental semantics aligned with the causal question (independent‑generation semantics when measuring verifier causal effect), (2) budgeting model calls to permit independent sampling or repair search, (3) expanding adversary protocols to include stronger and adaptive manipulations when robustness is a concern, and (4) instrumenting cross‑checks between deterministic verifier PASS and emulator outcomes to detect potential false‑safe scenarios.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe), yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). This null paired contrast is explained artifact‑wise by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics combined with deterministic verifier passes: the single shared candidates passed validation in every task and no repairs were invoked, so the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to change the paired outcome. The archived preregistration, execution manifest, validator traces, and analysis artifacts fully support these conclusions. We provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future GVR evaluations to produce informative paired contrasts (independent generation semantics, larger repair budgets, stronger adversaries, and expanded verifier coverage).

disclosure_statement: Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini via the registered adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0d...). The human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; all literature review, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock. The registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); under that contract paired divergences could only arise if the shared candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. Execution accounting (archived) records planned episodes = 480, completed episodes = 480, complete paired tasks = 240, and observed hosted model calls = 240. The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The execution manifest, per‑task traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived with this study to enable reproducibility and independent inspection. No manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompt templates, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and made verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive attackers.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 encodes a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected and verifier PASS vs emulator mismatches (planned sensitivity checks) did not occur in this run.
